newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists defend role in leftist majority.
newsitem.headline: French Communists defend role in leftist majority.

text.p: French Communist leader Robert Hue denied on Monday that party members' criticisms of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin were meant as a warning the Communists might desert the governing leftist coalition.
"Absolutely not," he said in a broadcast interview when asked whether the criticisms were intended as a warning.
"I consider the Communist Party today to be entirely within its role of a party which participates in the majority and in the government," Hue told France Inter radio.
He said Communist comments were intended as constructive suggestions, "to see what can be done right away to move forward".

He spoke a day after lunching with Jospin in the first meeting of the two men since a leftist alliance including Socialists, Communists and Greens won an upset parliamentary election victory five weeks ago.
Jospin was scheduled to meet Communist members of the National Assembly at 3 p.m. (1300 GMT).

After his talks with Jospin, Hue had publicly urged the prime minister to take immediate action to combat France's near-record 12.5 percent unemployment rather than put off decisions on key jobs programmes until the autumn.

Earlier, several Communist parliamentarians, joined by some Socialists, had protested loudly when Jospin let carmaker Renault close a plant in Vilvoorde, Belgium, despite a campaign promise to review the matter.
Hue said he had no intention of threatening the government and meant only to help with policy suggestions.

But he reiterated Communist opposition to France joining European monetary union, saying the austerity required to meet the criteria for a transition to the euro would prevent the adoption of needed but costly social programmes.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn reiterated on Tuesday that European economic and monetary union was impossible without French participation.
In an interview with Radio Luxembourg, Strauss-Kahn also reaffirmed that Paris intended to stick to the timetable for adopting the single currency from January 1, 1999.
Hue said there remained "a serious difference" between the Socialists and Communists over the euro.

Meeting the Maastricht treaty criteria for monetary union, which limit public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product, "would have serious consequences in terms of austerity and employment," he said.

Jospin, whose alliance of Socialists, Communists and Greens took power just five weeks ago after an upset parliamentary election victory, had ruled out more austerity during the campaign, vowing that jobs would be his top priority.
But after taking office, he put off decisions until autumn on how to implement the potentially costly jobs programmes he had promised during the campaign.
He said keeping these promises would have to await results of an audit of public finances expected later this month.
French officials have already hinted, however, that the audit would find the public deficit to be above the Maastricht treaty's three percent ceiling.
That raised the possibility of further delays in the jobs programmes or of new austerity measures needed to qualify for the euro.
